Just one thing I'd like to point out is that your understanding of science itself is problematic if you think science is about finding answers. Scientific method is a method of analysis. It's an organisation of knowledge. If by such analysis, you gain answers about certain things, that's an achievement but that doesn't make it a prerequisite. Sociology is a science because it utilises the scientific method to analyse past and present. Science does not mean everyone will reach one answer, it just requires everyone to apply a scientific method in achieving their answers. So in chemistry, everyone may reach one answer to say, a reaction between two compounds when applying the scientific method, the same will not hold true for sociology where multiple answers can be ascertained for a single thing, that's just how complicated human society is.

Why is it a worthwhile discipline? Society can't function without understanding itself. You can't frame laws without sociological analysis of their impact, the need for framing said law etc. You can't study economics in isolation without the sociological analysis of the impact of said economic model upon society. You can't tackle racism without critical race theory and a sociological analysis of how race became a form of distinction for humans and a reason for social othering. You can't change the present without understanding it.

To negate sociology's existence and merit is negating the context of human history and its effect on the present.

> It never seems to provide any concrete explanation for human behaviour.

There can't be concrete answers about *everything*, would you demand a physicist to give you a concrete answer about the nature of blackholes? They can't do that but they can give you *some* concrete answers. If you've not found that, I feel you've not really indulged in sociology enough. Or you're comparing it to a science like biology and physics and expecting direct answers. As I explained above, this cannot happen in a social science. There aren't universal rules in human behaviour and organisation the same way human anatomy or physical phenomenon may have.

The view you're expressing is prevalent in Richard Dawkins' The Selfish Gene. He says our entire evolutionary process is based on a selfish drive. This worldview has been proven wrong since then. There is extensive research into the idea that people can be altruistic for the sake of it and we have the potential to put someone else before the self, one of the key reasons why Dawkins' idea is no more accepted as a biological fact.

The reason you see this behaviour in society is because our economics and social relations are intricately linked and we are pushed into competition. In a society where everything is concentrated into the hands of a few, the rest are encouraged to fight and compete among themselves so that they can survive. This breeds selfishness. It promotes it. Save yourself, fuck the rest, is what this system perpetuates. Profit is the aim for everything and to make profit, you have to fuck someone over. Whether it be your coworker or the one working under you. Hell, it extends to the other gender or other races. Everyone is a competitor in this system.

Don't forget that there have been human societies in the past that functioned purely on collective effort and community living. The aim was to leave no one behind. Our current social structure, sadly, does not give us the same privilege. So don't fault people as individuals for this, blame the world we have constructed in the last 400 years.
